newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - EU taxes wheat exports, closes export season.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU taxes wheat exports, closes export season.

text.p: European Union, anxious to protect domestic supplies in the face of mounting drought fears and volatile prices, on Thursday slapped taxes on its daily exports of soft wheat grain and flour.
The move, which brings this season's wheat exports to a halt, pushed Chicago wheat futures higher. The May contract rose 1-1/4 to $4.33-1/2 after the news hit the market.
The move to restrict wheat exports follows a surge in world prices over fears that drought in Europe and frost in the United States may hurt 1997 grain crops.
"With market uncertainty about future supplies, we believe it is prudent to curb exports to ensure adequate supplies at reasonable prices," Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
"Our export prices are well already below world market prices. We had to prevent European wheats from flowing to the the world market," one EU grain official said.
Thursday, the EU's grain committee imposed taxes of 15 Ecus per tonne on daily exports of soft wheat grain and of 20 Ecus per tonne on flour exports.
Soft wheat prices have soared above EU intervention levels by 25.5 percent in Italy, 20 percent in Britain, 15 percent in France and by 9.5 percent in Germany.
Fears that a prolonged dry spell in Europe could curtail crop yields drove the price rise.
Last week the European Union closed its weekly wheat export tenders in a bid to dampen domestic prices.
But it had kept a more flexible daily export channel open, allowing traders to place bids to export wheat grain or flour with nil value refund.
Because these refunds could not be set in advance, this left exporters exposed to a tax, if the EU chose to impose one.

European Union started the 1996/97 season with a wheat export tax when stocks were low and prices high. But wheat export refunds were restored in mid-September as prospects of bumper crops in the main producing countries put a dampener on world prices.
European Union also refused Thursday all bids to export free market barley in a move to keep domestic barley prices under control. But it kept the weekly bidding channel for barley open.
"The situation on the European market did not justify granting a refund," an EU grain official said.
French barley for April-June delivery into Rouen had peaked at 910 francs per tonne ahead of the tender results.
In France, exporters had bid to ship 233,000 tonnes of barley and some were awaiting refunds to help cover recent sales to Iran, Cyprus, and Libya.
